approachQuestion.prompt:
Prize Catalog
A read-only array H is guaranteed to be a valid binary max-heap of n distinct integer prizes: children of index i are 2i+1 and 2i+2 when present. Return its k largest prizes in descending order. Example: H=[20,15,18,3,10,17,12], k=3 → [20,18,17].

2 ≤ n ≤ 1000000; 1 ≤ k ≤ floor(n/2). Integers fit signed 32 bits. Input supports constant-time random access. Heap validity is guaranteed and need not be verified. Return values only in separate output storage. Which approach best meets this contract?
constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 1000000; 1 ≤ k ≤ floor(n/2). Integers fit signed 32 bits. Input supports constant-time random access. Heap validity is guaranteed and need not be verified. Return values only in separate output storage.

options.text: Put the root’s index in an auxiliary max-heap keyed by H[index]. Repeatedly remove its maximum index, emit its prize, and add that node’s existing child indices, until k prizes are emitted.
options.feedback: Every unexplored subtree is dominated by its root candidate. A larger hidden descendant therefore cannot be missed before its candidate ancestor is selected; only newly exposed children need to enter the frontier.

options.text: Copy the entire supplied heap, then remove its maximum k times.
options.feedback: This preserves order correctly but copies every node even when few prizes are requested.

options.text: Return the first k array entries sorted descending.
options.feedback: The example’s first three values give 20,18,15, omitting hidden 17; breadth-first position is not full prize order.

options.text: Follow only the larger child after each emission and never revisit the other branch.
options.feedback: For H=[20,19,18,1,2,17,16], k=3, following one branch can omit 18, which must be third.

A max-heap parent dominates every descendant, so exposing children only after selecting their parent preserves all possible next maxima. The auxiliary frontier explores k winners rather than scanning n stored prizes.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze A with an initially one-entry binary candidate heap and k output iterations. Let n and k be as above. Each candidate stores an input index and constant-size key. Random input reads and output writes are counted; the input is not copied or verified. Choose the tightest time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Use the tightest worst-case bound for the whole input unless amortized or expected accounting is explicitly specified. Comparing or moving a record and arithmetic on machine words take constant time.

Exclude supplied input and returned output from auxiliary space. Count working arrays, queues, tables and call stacks. Output storage is separate and is not used as workspace. Heap repairs and traversals are iterative. No hashing is used unless explicitly stated.

options.text: O(k log(k+1)) time, O(k) auxiliary space
O(n + k log(n+1)) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(n log(n+1)) time, O(k) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: At most two child candidates per selected node bound work and storage by k.
details: Each chosen index inserts at most two children, so there are O(k) candidate operations and at most k+1 live frontier entries. Heap repairs give O(k log(k+1)) worst-case time, attainable on broad heap frontiers, and O(k) auxiliary space. No scan over n occurs. Even k=1 reads only the root and constant many children.
“O(n + k log(n+1)) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: This is the full-copy method, while A explores only exposed candidates.
“O(k) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The candidate frontier can grow with k, and repairs are not constant-time.
“O(n log(n+1)) time, O(k) auxiliary space”: The input’s guaranteed heap invariant permits skipping most of its nodes.
